title: Kim’s Second Byungjin: 21 Years After the Six-Party Talks Agreement
gist: Marking 21 years since the 2005 Six-Party Talks Joint Statement, CSIS argues North Korea has rejected every front-loaded, step-by-step offer and is now pursuing a 'second byungjin': expanding its nuclear arsenal while seeking normalization as a de facto nuclear power. A Trump-Kim summit has some pragmatic value, but abandoning CVID would harm alliances; meanwhile US-Japan-South Korea deterrence is working, as shown by Beijing, Moscow and Pyongyang's anger.

insights.claim: The 2005 September 19 Joint Statement offered North Korea security assurances, diplomatic recognition and energy/economic aid in an action-for-action exchange for denuclearization, but was silent on its uranium enrichment program.

insights.claim: Talks lost momentum in 2008 when Pyongyang omitted its highly enriched uranium program from its declaration and refused verification; since 2012 North Korea has consistently refused meaningful nuclear dialogue.
